title: Invest Like the Best — Uber CEO on AI, Autonomous Vehicles, and the Future of Transportation
text: Dara Khosrowshahi (Uber CEO) on AI, Autonomous Vehicles, and the Physical Internet — Research Memo Thesis Uber's durable moat in the AV era is demand aggregation — not the technology stack — and the 30% utilization premium it delivers to AV partners is the empirical anchor for that claim. The company is simultaneously deploying AI at a pace that is already blowing through budgets and making engineers "superhuman," but Khosrowshahi's explicit framing is that efficiency gains will be competed away via lower rider prices and higher driver earnings rather than converted to shareholder margin. The central non-consensus call: AV operators need Uber more than Uber needs any single AV operator, inverting the standard disintermediation narrative. Key Points AV Platform Strategy - AVs on Uber's network run 30% busier than those operating off-platform — the single hardest data point in the transcript and Khosrowshahi's core argument for why AV manufacturers will partner rather than go direct. - Uber has 30+ AV partnerships (Waymo, Nuro, Lucid, Nvidia cited) and is explicitly not betting on a single winner; the strategy is to be the go-to-market layer for any "digital driver." - Commercial robotaxi pilots in London launch before year-end 2026 ; Khosrowshahi frames European regulators as increasingly entrepreneurial after falling behind. - AV manufacturing cost-down is blocked by the absence of a Foxconn-equivalent in the Western hemisphere; Khosrowshahi states Chinese players' manufacturing scale capabilities are unrivaled (scoped to cost/scale manufacturing, not autonomy software — Waymo still referenced as a lead partner). AI Deployment - Uber blew through its entire AI budget in a single quarter ; current posture is explore-with-frontier-models, then migrate to cheaper models at scale. - Developers in India are generating 10× their prior code-commit volume via autonomous agents (commits are the disclosed metric — a limited proxy; not equivalent to 10× output quality). - Search/matching models are 10,000× larger than legacy models; destination prediction now correct ~ 75% of the time , driving dispatch efficiency and dynamic pricing. - Headcount additions being "metered" as engineer throughput rises — explicit labor-for-compute substitution already underway. Drone Delivery - Battery energy density and payload capacity are the binding constraints explaining why commercial drone delivery hasn't materialized at scale yet. - Khosrowshahi forecasts drone food delivery at real commercial scale within 2–5 years , with delivery initially costing more than human delivery; the category normalizes within 5–10 years (cost-competitiveness vs. human delivery not claimed). - 10–15 minute delivery windows cited as the consumer expectation reset if drones scale. Multi-Product Flywheel - 13% of Eats bookings originate from mobility customers — a disclosed cross-platform attach rate. - Uber One has 50 million members ; hotel/travel expansion follows trains after seeing "the same retention benefits." - 1.5 billion trips made outside riders' home cities — the data wedge underpinning the travel product. - $10B+ free cash flow on 10B+ trips annually, with Khosrowshahi explicitly describing Uber as a low-margin business where AI gains are targeted at price cuts and earner income rather than margin expansion. Macro/Regulatory Premortem - Khosrowshahi's stated premortem: AI and AVs generate public backlash if they visibly destroy jobs or raise electricity costs without inclusive access — he flags this as a real rollout risk, not a distant scenario. Best Quotes "AVs on our network are 30% busier than those that aren't, which makes a huge difference in ROI for those expensive cars." — Dara Khosrowshahi The single hardest quantitative data point in the transcript. Directly quantifies Uber's demand-aggregation moat; compresses AV operator payback periods and anchors the partnership-over-disintermediation thesis. "We blew through our AI budget in a quarter. We are going to meter headcount increases because as my engineers get more efficient, their throughput is increasing. They're becoming superhuman. There's a significant cost to that." — Dara Khosrowshahi Confirms AI compute is a real, already-materializing OpEx line — not a future investment. The headcount metering signal is a leading indicator of labor-for-compute substitution with ambiguous margin implications. "We're using the more expensive models to explore, but once we scale, we'll look to bring in more efficient models on a token basis." — Dara Khosrowshahi Explicit price-sensitivity to model tiers. Uber is a price-taker on inference today; this is both a near-term margin risk and a signal that the frontier model revenue pool faces compression as enterprise workloads commoditize. "We need a low-cost player in the Western hemisphere; the Chinese players' capabilities are unrivaled at this point." — Dara Khosrowshahi Unprompted acknowledgment of Chinese manufacturing superiority at scale. Embeds a structural cost-down risk into the trillion-dollar AV marketplace thesis — if Western manufacturing doesn't emerge, the price-decline curve flattens. Disagreements & Conviction T1 — AV disintermediation vs. coopetition (HIGH CONVICTION, WELL-ANCHORED) Khosrowshahi's view: AV operators will partner because the 30% utilization premium changes unit economics decisively. The conventional short thesis on UBER assumes AV operators (Waymo) build direct demand and cut out the aggregator. His analogy to OTAs and hotel chains is historically apt. The conviction is high but explicitly hedged: "It won't be black or white." The structural fragility: the utilization premium shrinks as Waymo's own installed base grows. The 30% figure applies now; its durability in a mature market is unverified. T2 — Platform-for-earners vs. AV displacement (UNACKNOWLEDGED INTERNAL CONTRADICTION) Khosrowshahi cites 10M+ earners as Uber's societal impact in one breath and trillion-dollar AV/drone displacement

title: Invest Like the Best — Why the AI Boom Is Just Getting Started
text: Whale Rock Capital / Anthropic — Research Memo Thesis Frontier AI is consolidating into a three-player oligopoly (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) mirroring the AWS/Azure/GCP cloud structure, after ~50 foundational-model startups washed out. Agentic coding is the first proven revenue unlock — a ~$500B TAM from developers alone — and enterprise AI remains at ~10 basis points of knowledge-worker adoption, placing it at the earliest phase of an exponential ramp. The highest-certainty trade is the hardware supply chain, whose visibility has structurally shifted from weeks to years; the non-consensus short is legacy application software, which Whale Rock entered 2026 net short on the thesis that CIO budgets are migrating to AI tokens faster than the market prices. Key Points Anthropic / Foundational Models - Investment made in August 2025 at a $180B valuation; ARR trajectory tracked as $100M → $1B → $9B; no visibility into 2026 numbers at entry. - Three-horse oligopoly thesis: Amazon "never showed up" as a serious model-layer competitor; Meta attempted entry and required a full reboot. The field of ~50–60 foundational-model startups has largely washed out. - Competitive moats cited: critical IP, enterprise brand, capital access, ecosystem (SDK / Claude for Work / orchestration layer / harness), and — explicitly — recursive self-improvement : Anthropic feeds Claude Code outputs back into model training, accelerating its own capability pace. - Vertical differentiation undermines the commodity thesis: guest cites Anthropic as superior for private equity/finance tasks; Google Gemini as superior for PDF ingestion. These are task-level examples, not structural proof, but they support persistent pricing power. - Open-source risk is bounded by compute capital, not algorithms: open-source models can close to within ~5 percentage points of frontier benchmarks but cannot leapfrog because they lack training compute. The moat is financial scale, not IP secrecy. - Bear case acknowledged: if frontier scaling stalls, open-source closes the gap and the model layer becomes a race to zero. Agentic Coding — The "True Unlock" - Both André Karpathy and Linus Torvalds publicly reversed their positions: Karpathy previously estimated AI wrote 20% of code with 80% handwritten; after the latest Claude Code release, he now writes code only in English. Torvalds made a parallel flip. - Unit economics: internal Anthropic users spending ~$100/day on tokens → ~$20–30K/year annualized ARPU. Applied to 20M global coders: ~$500B TAM from coding alone. - Claude Code is described as the first tool to operate "almost completely agentically" — a qualitative step change from first-gen tools like Microsoft Copilot (~$20/month, grammar-level assistance). S-Curve / Adoption Positioning - Two-tier penetration claim (distinct data points): - Infrastructure layer : guest estimates ~10% penetrated. - Knowledge-worker AI adoption : ~10 basis points, per Sundar [Google CEO; last name inferred]. - Anthropic at ~14–15M DAUs as of episode date. - Guest projects 10bps → 15%+ knowledge-worker adoption over four years, calling the shape an "L-curve" (near-vertical) rather than an S-curve at this stage. - Analogized to Internet 1.0 in 1998: "you knew you needed a website, but it was hard to build." Software Short - Whale Rock reduced software from ~40–50% of portfolio to near zero; entered 2026 net short legacy application software. - Mechanism: CIO priority list has shifted — Anthropic token spend yields faster measurable ROI than legacy SaaS seat renewals. Incumbent AI features are generating 1–2% of software revenue. - New screening heuristic: "Rule of 40 for AI" = % of sales that are AI-native × AI market share. Legacy software scores near zero; the threshold the guest cites as strong is ~60. Hardware Decommoditization - AI workloads growing ~10× per year vs. a flat Moore's Law curve — the data center is being pushed to physical limits for the first time in 40 years. - Visibility has shifted from "we'll call you next week" to multi-year roadmap co-design. Named examples: Celestica (sole-source Google TPU server), Corning (fiber), Elite Materials (copper-clad laminate). - Equipment cited at $200–300K per liquid-cooled AI server; switching cost is effectively prohibitive once designed in. Firm/Portfolio Context - Nvidia bought in 2023 at ~4× earnings; Tesla in 2019 at ~5×; AWS was "essentially free" inside Amazon's retail multiple. - Framework: S-curve positioning + competitive advantage + underappreciated earnings power → buy best companies in the world at low P/E because exponential earnings are invisible to consensus. - Fund lineup: long-short (original), long-only (now larger), opt-in privates, and newly launched Mega Cap Tech Fund targeting structurally underweight large-cap tech positions. Best Quotes 1. "We started hearing that people who could use it unfettered — even within Anthropic at that time — people were spending $100 a day on tokens, which if you do the math comes out to $20,000 or $30,000 a year. If you think about how many coders there are in the world — 20 million — you've got a half-a-trillion-dollar market just from coding alone." — Alex (Whale Rock) Significance: The load-bearing unit-economics chain for the Anthropic investment: internal spend rate → annualized ARPU → TAM. Every number is specific and checkable; this is the quantified foundation of the thesis, not a top-down market-size assertion. 2. "Five years ago, we might have had 40% or 50% of our portfolio in software. Pretty quickly, we realized their AI products were not very good. They weren't moving the needle. Nobody could charge for them. We basically sold almost all of our application software. Entering this year, we were actually net short." — Alex (Whale Rock) Significance: Position-level specificity — a major tech fund running net short legacy software is a strong, non-consensus allocation signal. This is a decision, not a view. 3. "Karpathy said last year's code

title: Monetary Matters — China’s Supply Shock: The Upcoming Event That Will Ruin Memory Chip Stocks
text: Asian Equities Dispersion — Korea Small Caps, Memory Bubble, and the China Governance Trap — Research Memo Thesis Korean memory stocks (SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics) are in a speculative bubble with consensus 2028 net profit estimates implying commodity producers become the most profitable companies on earth — a valuation that will be challenged by Chinese DRAM supply arriving from 2027 onward. The same index concentration that has inflated memory names has force-sold Korean small caps to single-digit P/Es, where a 2025 director-liability reform creates an independent activism catalyst that does not require the memory bubble to deflate. China is not a compensating trade: the property bust was deliberate government policy, private companies operate under Communist Party shadow boards (enacted 2020), and insiders are selling en masse. Key Points Korean Memory — Bubble Call - Consensus 2028 combined net profit estimates for SK Hynix and Samsung are $200–250B USD, which would make them the most profitable companies in the world — for commodity producers. Fritzell calls this "extremely speculative" and "not prudent." - KOSPI is now 50–60% concentrated in two memory chip stocks. iShares MSCI Korea ETF is up ~255% over one year (host-sourced figure, confirmed in transcript). - Fritzell draws a 1999 US analogy explicitly: value stocks sold, retail doubling into momentum names, speculation reminiscent of COVID 2021 in Korea. - Timing is tentative: "eventually, maybe from the end of this year or early 2027" — his own language includes "maybe," making this a scenario, not a committed call. Chinese DRAM Supply — The Exit Mechanism - Yangtze Memory and peers are expanding capacity rapidly. Fritzell states he is "very confident" Chinese competitors "will come with new supply in 2027 onwards." - Analogy: solar panels, EVs, batteries — China excels at hardware scale-up. Memory is standardized enough (three to five global competitors) that pricing discipline will be difficult to maintain once Chinese yields improve. - Named leading indicator: TrendForce enterprise DRAM spot prices — Fritzell's stated exit signal. - Caveat: Fritzell also says he "is not able to confidently predict how the cycle is going to move" — the supply response is directionally high-conviction, the timing less so. TSMC / Logic Chips — More Sustainable, Still Speculative - Logic chips are "a completely different calculus" — genuine long-run bottleneck, TSMC has not raised prices aggressively, structural moat intact. - However, Taiwan retail speculation has probably exceeded 2020 levels (Fritzell's word: "probably"); average Taiwan market P/E ~30. He explicitly says "we are some way through this AI boom." - Western investors are bifurcated: they ignore invasion risk for TSMC specifically while ignoring all other Taiwanese stocks. Korean Small Caps — The Preferred Trade - During the large-cap memory rally, Korean small caps have sold off. Single-digit P/E companies in consumer, industrials, and software are available. - Structural catalyst: As of 2025, Korean directors are legally liable to act in the best interest of all minority shareholders — a datable legal change. Activist capital is actively hiring in Korea now. - Playbook mirrors Japan post-2023 governance reform, but at earlier stage and cheaper entry multiples. Fritzell: "If you're a stock picker, it's time to move on from Japan and look towards Korea." - Specific chaebol headwinds acknowledged: 50% inheritance tax, dividend tax structure — but the 2025 liability law is concrete. Named Long: NICE Information Service (Korean FICO analog) - Dominant credit score provider; every bank loan query triggers a fee payment — described as a "toll bridge." - Single-digit P/E; growth is margin-accretive. Fritzell holds it and discloses the position. - Relative value: trades at approximately one-third of FICO's multiple with a comparable business model. - Note: Multiple entities exist within the NICE Group in Korea; the specific listed vehicle was not ticker-attributed in the transcript. Entity verification required before any position inquiry. China — Personal Avoidance, Not a Structural Pronouncement - Fritzell is personally disillusioned and avoiding China. He does not use the word "uninvestable." [Inference: he is effectively uninvested in China based on the totality of his remarks.] - New residential construction down 70%+ since 2021. Key framing: "The government did this on purpose" — deliberate deleveraging, not an accidental crisis. This changes recovery timing calculus. - 2020 law: Private companies required to have a Communist Party committee functioning as a shadow board. Fritzell: "It makes you question how independent these companies are." This is a datable structural governance constraint predating the property bust. - Antitrust actions against companies like Trip.com are unpredictable. Jack Ma as exemplar of unquantifiable political risk. - Insider selling en masse in China; insider buying strong in Southeast Asia. Nintendo - Down ~50%; headwinds are real: DRAM input cost inflation, thin 2026 holiday content pipeline, GTA 6 boosting Sony. - Fritzell sees a 2027 setup: Zelda movie + potential 3D Mario. Language is tentative ("it feels like we are getting to a point where sentiment cannot get much worse") — this is an observation, not a conviction call. No valuation anchor provided. Southeast Asia Geopolitics - Singapore and Philippines: pro-US. Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand: closer to China on trade and infrastructure. - Fritzell: "A new Cold War is forming, and the lines haven't been drawn yet." East Asia got wealthy through US trade; losing that access would impact growth. - Insider buying strong across SE Asia broadly. title: Monetary Matters — The Oil Market Has One Month Left Before A “Rupture” Occurs | Kpler’s Matt Smith
text: Strait of Hormuz Crisis: Physical Oil Market Breakdown — Research Memo Thesis The global oil market is masking a structural supply crisis through two mechanisms: a ~9 mb/d collapse in global refinery runs that suppresses visible crude inventory draws, and China's temporary exit from crude buying that has freed ~4.5 mb/d for other markets. Both buffers are finite. Matt Smith (Director of Research, Kepler — a research platform focused on commodities, particularly energy) identifies Cushing tank bottoms and U.S. export curtailment as the specific, trackable trigger for repricing, forecasting the inflection in July 2026. The $200 oil thesis is his explicit, on-record call; the critical caveat is that he simultaneously concedes a prolonged sub-$200 stalemate is "a real possibility." Key Points Supply Arithmetic - The Strait of Hormuz has been closed ~3+ months; 15 mb/d of crude exports plus ~5 mb/d of products are blocked - Saudi Arabia has rerouted ~4 mb/d around the blockage; net crude supply loss is therefore ~11 mb/d (the 15 mb/d blocked minus ~4 mb/d rerouted) - Over 13 mb/d of production is now shut in; onshore storage at origin is full - Even if the Strait reopens tomorrow, months of sequencing delay follow: clear full tankers → drain onshore storage → restart refineries → ramp production — this shock is 4× the size of feared Russian supply loss in 2022 The Masking Mechanism - Global refineries cut runs by ~9 mb/d, absorbing ~82% of the supply loss; only 2 mb/d shows up as inventory draws - The market reads low inventory draws as manageable; the real signal is the refinery collapse behind that number - 84% of all global crude inventory draws are concentrated in just two countries: the U.S. and Japan — the rest of the world's apparent stability is a function of opaque reporting, not genuine buffer - India has only ~20 days of storage cover; non-OECD vulnerability is structurally high even though it doesn't appear in inventory statistics The China Factor - China (~11 mb/d importer) halted crude buying; has cut refinery runs rather than drawing crude inventories - The ~4.5 mb/d China freed for other markets — including reselling West African barrels it had already bought — is the single largest shock-absorber preventing a price spike - China cannot stay out indefinitely; re-entry into a market with near-operational-minimum inventories is the demand-side catalyst, independent of any Strait resolution U.S. as Marginal Supplier and Imminent Constraint - U.S. refiners tweaked yields to maximize jet fuel production (responding to Europe's loss of 45–50% of its jet fuel supply from the Middle East); U.S. jet fuel hit its highest level of the year - That yield shift has come at direct cost: gasoline and distillate inventories are "absolutely tanking"; U.S. distillate inventories are at a 23-year low - Cushing, Oklahoma: inventories falling ~1 mb/d/week for 8–9 weeks; approaching operational tank bottoms (~20% capacity), which is the mechanical floor below which oil cannot be pumped - WTI/Brent narrowing (WTI firming relative to Brent) is already underway; record U.S. exports of 5.6 mb/d are falling below 5 mb/d in June as barrels dry up - U.S. export curtailment removes the last meaningful swing supplier to Europe and Asia — "when the U.S. stops sending those barrels out, that's when the music stops" The IEA Inventory Bear Case Is Structurally Misleading - Bears cite ~8 billion barrels of IEA-tracked global inventory; Smith argues this is largely operational oil that cannot physically be drawn — identical logic to Cushing's 20% floor - The metric is analytically broken; accessible, pumpable inventories are a fraction of the headline Escalation Tail Risk - Iran retains the option to close Bab el-Mandeb via the Houthis, forcing all tankers around the Cape of Good Hope — Smith describes this as "a disaster" but it is not his base case Pricing Paradox - Sub-$100 oil four months into an 11 mb/d supply shock: Smith calls this explicitly irrational — "that defies logic" - Partial explanation: China's exit, market illiquidity from policy uncertainty ("nobody wants to trade because they don't know what's going to happen in a minute if the President tweets") - SPR releases in the U.S. and Japan have cushioned the shock but are finite Best Quotes 1. "Simplistically, we have supply down about 11 million barrels per day on average over the last three months. To offset that, we have seen about 9 million barrels a day of refinery runs being cut on a global basis. The difference, those 2 million barrels a day, is inventory draws." — Matt Smith Significance: Quantifies the demand-destruction mechanism that is obscuring the true supply shock. Low visible inventory draws are not a sign of adequacy — they are a sign that 9 mb/d of refinery capacity has been sacrificed. 2. "We are four months into this, and prices are below $100. That defies logic." — Matt Smith Significance: The analyst with the most granular flow data in this conversation is explicitly flagging a mispricing. This is the core investment signal of the interview — not a bear case being rebutted, but a bull case being asserted by someone who tracks the physical data. 3. "I'll pick it up. I'll take the educational hit of being wrong. Something is going to break. We have to reach the point where the price of that last available barrel rises high enough to kill demand." — Matt Smith Significance: Rare on-record conviction call for $200 oil from a named commodity researcher, staked as a reputational commitment. Immediately relevant caveat: in the same interview he acknowledges a prolonged sub-$200 stalemate as "a real possibility" — the two statements are unreconciled. 4. It's a series of ducks you have

title: Monetary Matters — America’s $205 Billion Fund You’ve Never Heard Of | Conor Coleman
text: U.S. Development Finance Corporation — Strategy Pivot & Deal Flow Research Memo Thesis The DFC is undergoing a structural transformation from a concessional development lender into an active Wall Street-style strategic investor — deploying equity, mezzanine, and structured notes alongside legacy products — with $25B in authorized capacity over six years (~$4.2B/year). The mechanism for competing with China's BRI ($125B deployed last year alone) is a private-sector multiplier model requiring 3–4× capital co-investment per DFC dollar, making DFC a recurring anchor investor and deal-flow source for EM-focused alternative asset managers, sovereigns, and listed miners. Three near-term investable signals are already in the public domain: a named listed-equity holding (Syrah Resources, ASX: SYR), a named reinsurance counterparty (Chubb, CB), and a $1.8B (or $1.2B — see Confidence Zones) critical minerals vehicle with Abu Dhabi's ADQ. Key Points Mandate & Structure - DFC is the US government's international investment arm, reauthorized post-2025 with expanded toolkit: now includes common equity, structured equity, mezzanine, and structured notes in addition to prior senior secured loans, political risk insurance, and fund/bank intermediation. - Statutory investment cap is $25B over six years; 90% (~$22.5B) must be deployed in World Bank low-to-middle-income countries — a binding geographic constraint absent from most public commentary on DFC. This floors the vast majority of deployment in EM/frontier. - Seven priority sectors: (1) critical minerals, (2) transport/logistics infrastructure, (3) energy, (4) technology & telecom, (5) food security & agriculture, (6) healthcare, (7) financial services. Coleman identifies the first four as "bigger ticket items" under current administration priorities. - Target geographies: Latin America/Caribbean, Central Asia, Eastern Europe, Indo-Pacific; Africa currently 25% of Coleman's personal portfolio. - CEO: Ben Black (Senate-confirmed). Board: Commerce (Lutnick), Treasury (Bessent), State (Rubio). Not every transaction requires board sign-off; delegated authority exists at CEO level. Belt-and-Road Gap - China deployed $125B through BRI last year — more than five times DFC's total authorized cap. Coleman acknowledges the gap; the multiplier thesis (2–4× private capital per DFC dollar) is the only credible path to volume parity. It is stated as aspiration; no historical mobilization ratio is cited. Strait of Hormuz Reinsurance - Structured in under one month (DFC's fastest-ever deal) in partnership with Chubb as lead insurer ; DFC provides ~50% reinsurance on hull & machinery, cargo, and P&I policies. - Not yet live. Launch contingent on US military confirmation that operational security (Navy escort) can be guaranteed; Coleman confirms the financial portal is ready. The trigger is outside DFC's control — the military's decision, not DFC's. - Precedent structure: a similar product was previously used for Ukraine war risk. Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF) - Perpetual-capital vehicle; seeded at ~$150M+ via equal US/Ukraine government contributions; replenished by royalty streams from greenfield hydrocarbons, critical minerals, and energy projects in Ukraine. - First investment: Sign Technologies, described as an "emergent technology company" offering "components to certain drone capabilities" in Ukraine. Defense-adjacent characterization is analyst inference; Coleman's framing is neutral. - Pipeline: 200+ deals submitted; 3–4 more investments expected in 2026. One closed out of 200+ submitted — conversion rate is early-stage, Coleman attributes to pace of setup not pipeline quality. - Both greenfield and brownfield mineral projects are eligible. Co-investment vehicles with private capital (PE, SWFs, quasi-multilaterals) are being structured. Orion CMC - DFC, Orion, and ADQ have "each" invested $600M into a joint vehicle focused on critical minerals upstream/midstream — total equity likely $1.8B if three parties, $1.2B if "each" refers to two parties; transcript does not resolve this ambiguity. - The host introduced a $500M debt component ("$600M in equity investments as well as $500M in debt"); Coleman's response addressed only the equity layer and never confirmed or addressed the debt figure. The $500M debt component is unconfirmed in the transcript. - DFC holds veto rights on offtake to ensure routing to US or allied partners — an explicit supply-chain exclusion mechanism targeting China. Public Equity - DFC executed its first debt-for-equity transaction, taking an equity stake in Syrah Resources (ASX: SYR) , which has a graphite mine in Mozambique and an anode materials processing facility in the US. Named explicitly; directly actionable. Semiconductor / AI - When asked whether DFC would invest in semiconductor supply chain or AI, Coleman said "Of course." No elaboration, no program details, no timeline. Treat as disclosed openness, not announced program. Deployment Conviction - Coleman: "I have no worries that we're going to hit that deployment amount under Ben's leadership." Full $25B expected deployed within the six-year authorization window. - Note: The host incorrectly stated the annual average as "$27.5 billion" (arithmetic error: $25B ÷ 6 = ~$4.2B/year). Coleman did not correct this on air. Best Quotes 1. The competitive gap — why the multiplier is mandatory, not aspirational "Last year, China invested $125 billion in that initiative, which is more than half of my total AUM. Our goal, if we really are to compete, is to bridge the gap by utilizing the United States' greatest strength, which is our private sector and our capital markets." — Connor Coleman Significance: Quantifies the structural impossibility of volume parity on government balance sheets alone; the 3–4× private multiplier is arithmetically necessary, not just strategic preference. title: Monetary Matters — Massive AI Crackdown Is Coming (It’s Simply Too Good) | David Woo
text: AI Capex Illusion, Frontier Model Regulation, and the Oil Trade — Research Memo Monetary Matters / David Woo, Independent Economist Thesis The AI equity rally is built on three compounding illusions: nominal capex growth that is input-price inflation masquerading as volume demand, ARR growth partially inflated by mandated corporate consumption that is already unwinding, and an assumption of open frontier-model monetization that Woo argues is already being administratively throttled. The bear case is not that AI fails technically — Woo uses it two hours daily — but that its most capable iteration is too dangerous to distribute at scale, making the monetization curve priced into $5T of Nasdaq re-rating since April structurally inaccessible. Simultaneously, he holds a long oil position predicated on a game-theoretic read that Trump's public deal urgency has hardened Iranian resolve, making a near-term Hormuz resolution less likely than the market prices. Key Points Capex Accounting Mechanics - Combined capex of the five hyperscalers (MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, ORCL, META) fell quarter-over-quarter in Q1 — the first such decline in three years — and the year-on-year growth rate decelerated; real-terms contraction is larger still given component price inflation. - The earnings illusion: hyperscalers expense capex via depreciation (~10% in purchase period); component suppliers (Micron, SK Hynix) book 100% of price increases as revenue. A $100 price increase on the same chip creates $90 of aggregate EPS growth with zero incremental economic activity. This is the same accounting rules applied to an unusual degree, not a manipulation — but the scale exaggerates AI-sector earnings momentum materially. - Capex-to-operating-income for the five hyperscalers has reached 135%, forcing Google (seeking $80–85B equity raise) and Meta to issue external capital — a structural break from the era of self-funded investment. - Google and Amazon offset their Q1 capex pickup with a revaluation of Anthropic holdings — Woo's characterization: "totally artificial." - Microsoft and Meta pulled back Q1 capex; Microsoft lost its OpenAI exclusivity and corporate Copilot adoption has been "worse than expected." - Increased capex guidance from hyperscalers largely reflects paying more for the same volumes, not building more capacity — the homebuilder analogy: same 10 homes, $7M instead of $5M. Demand Quality: Token-Maxing - Q1 AI consumption was inflated by corporate incentive structures (Amazon ranked engineers by AI usage), driving artificial demand — "token maxing." - Uber's COO stated publicly that the company burned its entire year's token budget in four months with little to show for it and is now pulling back. Woo relays this as a third-party data point, not firsthand knowledge. - Anthropic ARR grew from $9B to ~$42–44B, but Woo expects Q2 deceleration as token-maxing unwinds; Microsoft has also canceled most Claude licenses to push Copilot internally. - At least five LLM competitors now exist; the market is pricing "winner-take-all" dynamics in what is becoming a commoditized stack. Larry Ellison (per Woo citing Ellison) has said LLMs will commoditize because they train on the same public data. Regulatory Risk: The Core Bear Case - Woo argues frontier model regulation is the dominant AI equity risk on a 6–12 month horizon — conditionally: "If Claude 3.5 turns out to be too dangerous, the regulatory blowback will be the biggest risk to AI on a 6-to-12-month basis." - Claude 3.5 Sonnet (referenced as "Mythos" by the host) is, per Woo's unverified claim, distributed to only ~150 users — two months post-release, "it's gone nowhere." He characterizes this as de facto government control already in effect. - Cyberattacks "went through the roof" starting last December; Germany cited €300B in cyberattack costs in a single year — the only non-US data point in the transcript. - A Trump executive order reduced the model release cooldown from a proposed 90-day period to 30 days; Woo views this as inadequate but acknowledges it is regulatory motion already underway. - Woo's regulatory logic is security/control, not populism: once a recursive self-improving model is distributed to 500–1,000 users, provenance becomes uncontrollable. If China acquires it, the response options are nil. - Trump's delay in a full crackdown is attributed by Woo to a desire to let Anthropic/OpenAI IPO "while the market is in a bubble" — a temporary brake on what Woo views as inevitable restriction. - AI will become "a huge political issue heading into the midterms." Memory / HBM: Commodity Cycle, Not Secular Scarcity - HBM is structurally less complex than Nvidia logic chips; more competition exists and will increase. Chinese producers are advancing in DRAM and NAND flash; Woo states with high conviction they will reach HBM-level capability within 2–3 years. - Once new capacity comes online, prices drop quickly — the historical DRAM/NAND pattern. The "sold out into 2028" argument ignores the capacity cycle. - Short-term Q2 earnings deceleration is Woo's explicit near-term call. Training→Inference Shift - AI workloads are migrating from training (GPU-intensive, Nvidia-dominated) to inference (less compute-intensive, more producers for NAND, CPUs). This deflates the compute-intensity and pricing-power assumptions embedded in current Nvidia multiples. Oil / Iran - Woo is long oil, short equities, and short gold. - Hormuz throughput is "a very low number"; inventories are falling; unless a deal is reached, prices will "go through the roof." Trump's threshold is ~$150 before political pain forces action. - Game-theory problem: Trump's public urgency on a deal signals desperation to Iran, hardening their terms. Iran recently fired missiles at Israel — unprecedented — indicating they believe Trump is weak and are trying to drive a US-Israel wedge. Woo assesses near-term deal probability as low. - Most scenarios (no deal, escalation, partial deal with conditions) conv

title: No Priors — The Rise of the Full-Stack Builder and Hyper-Leveraged Generalist with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella
text: Microsoft Build 2026 — Satya Nadella on Frontier Intelligence, Harness Economics, and the Permission to Grow — Research Memo Thesis Microsoft's strategic bet is that every enterprise needs its own "frontier intelligence" — a private eval harness plus model-agnostic orchestration — rather than model ownership, and that this platform layer captures stickier economics than any individual model provider. The corollary is that benchmark-driven model competition commoditizes frontier labs faster than the market assumes, while the harness/eval layer and underlying SaaS data assets retain durable value. The social license to execute this buildout has a self-imposed 12–18 month tangibility deadline, after which permitting, regulatory, and public-opinion friction become binding constraints. Key Points Model & Platform Strategy - Microsoft's MAI model family is differentiated not by benchmark performance but by clean pre-training lineage plus a hill-climbing scaffold for building private specialist models. Nadella explicitly states public benchmarks "can be maxed" — private evaluation sets are the true IP moat. - The platform thesis: a platform is defined by creating more value outside it than it captures inside. Microsoft's job is to enable every company to "operate at the frontier with their own frontier intelligence." - Microsoft's harness (GitHub/Foundry) is explicitly model-agnostic — Llama, MAI, or any third-party model can plug in. This is a structural bet that model commoditization accelerates and platform stickiness migrates to the harness/eval layer. Agentic Deployment Reality - Coding agents are already productive enough to break the IDE. Nadella runs 100-agent sessions and states chat-only artifacts are unworkable: "We now have to rebuild the IDE." Canvas UI is a near-term forced transition. - Agent-captured "traces" of human-AI collaboration are the new enterprise IP: "Training a 'company veteran agent' that learns through those traces is incredibly valuable. It should essentially go on the balance sheet." This is a new asset-classification framework, not a metaphor. - Nadella himself is building long-running Foundry agents for chief-of-staff workflow monitoring — signals genuine internal adoption, not just positioning. Pricing & SaaS Economics - Per-user pricing is "an artifact of someone needing budget certainty." Consumption will be the next dominant model. - Outcome-based pricing structurally stalls: "People love outcome-based pricing until they actually have an outcome, and then it feels like giving away royalty." - Named admission: GitHub Copilot was mispriced as a per-seat product before the intensity of agent usage was understood. The repricing has already been executed. - The build-vs-buy equilibrium for AI-generated software will take "one full budget cycle" to resolve. Maintenance is the check on DIY euphoria: "AI can find security bugs, but someone has to fix them, and that burns tokens." SaaS Data Assets - The underlying data model and business logic of SaaS applications "are still robust and valuable." The disruption is in packaging, not annihilation. Microsoft 365 as an exposed database (Work IQ) is the concrete illustration: accessing design meeting notes via a GitHub repo query is "10x the value" but requires rearchitecting how requests are served. - Enterprises with "inflexible" software vendors face displacement; flexible incumbents with exposed data models earn a reprieve. Organizational Design - The Azure networking team's reconceptualization is Nadella's clearest organizational prescription: "Our job is not to do networking; it's to build the agentic system that does networking." They reframed their work as meta-work — building systems that do the work, not doing the work. He calls this "the lesson for any organization." - LinkedIn created a new "full-stack builder" discipline combining design, product, and engineering. Infrastructure roles (e.g., building RL environments for Excel) are becoming critical hard-engineering problems. Social License & Infrastructure - The host's intro monologue states Azure built more capacity in the last 15 months than in its first 15 years. (Attribution: host's framing — Nadella does not restate or confirm this figure in his own remarks.) - Nadella's societal deadline: "We have 12 to 18 months to make this tangible… whether it's health outcomes or the ability to run a local store more efficiently, people need to see it for themselves." This is a credibility cliff, not a hopeful observation. - Community-level permission framing (separate statement, same interview): "Unless we are principled about ensuring the benefits are felt at the community level, we won't have permission to grow. It has to be real: energy prices, water replenishment, training, jobs, and the tax base." Best Quotes Quote 1 — Satya Nadella "We know all the public evaluations out there can be maxed, so each company will have its own private evaluation. Every company having private evaluations might be the biggest intellectual property. If you have a private eval and you can switch from Model A to Model B and climb up, you're in control." Significance: Non-consensus indictment of public benchmarks as competitive signals. The durable moat is the eval harness, not the model — directly challenges the bull case for closed frontier labs. Quote 2 — Satya Nadella "People love outcome-based pricing until they actually have an outcome, and then it feels like giving away royalty. So that debate will continue. There is no one model to rule them all." Significance: Grounds consensus enthusiasm for outcome-based pricing with a behavioral observation from lived deployment experience. The GitHub Copilot reprice admission ("it was constructed as a per-user product before we understood the intensity of agent usage") makes this a closed empirical loop, not a musing. title: Odd Lots — Carmen Li's Plan to Build a Futures Market for Compute | Odd Lots
text: GPU Compute Futures — Research Memo (Odd Lots, Carmen Lee / Silicon Data & Compute Exchange) Thesis GPU compute is in transition from a procurement cost to a hedgeable commodity, with CME-listed financially settled futures set to launch within months. The near-term data contradicts two dominant consensus trades: inference costs are not falling to zero (token prices doubled in ~6 months), and GPU assets are not depreciating rapidly (H100 residual values near par as of last year). The instrument designed to enable hedging carries structural limitations — definitionally ambiguous volatility metrics, basis risk, and a significant index-provider/spot-marketplace conflict of interest — that a PM must price before treating CME GPU futures as a clean hedge. Key Points Market Structure - Carmen Lee is founder/CEO of both Silicon Data (the GPU price index provider; CME settles against this index) and Compute Exchange (a competing GPU spot marketplace) — a dual-hat structure with no firewall or governance controls discussed in the transcript. This conflict is cross-cutting and affects every claim about index integrity below. - GPU futures and options on CME are launching "in a couple of months" pending CFTC approval; financially settled, accessible through standard futures brokers with conventional margin. - OTC forward contracts can be "physically delivered" — but delivery consists of API access to specific configurations, not a wafer. This introduces counterparty credit and SLA performance risk that does not exist in commodity physical delivery. Index Methodology - Silicon Data ingests 150,000+ traded prices daily; total pricing database spans 8 million points from ~200 data sources. The daily ingestion draws from 100+ sources. - Normalization covers CPU, RAM, disk, geolocation, and memory bandwidth. Output is "highly correlated" but not equal to cloud provider prices — basis risk is structural and explicitly acknowledged. - Competing indices show divergent levels and trends. Lee's response: "the market always votes." Index methodology opacity is an unresolved risk; if the CME contract settles to Silicon Data's index and that index diverges materially from actual cloud costs, the futures fail their hedging function. Volatility & Fungibility - Lee cites "20–30% daily volatility" for A100s and H100s. Critical caveat (QA correction): the term "daily volatility" is Lee's phrasing; the transcript does not clarify whether this is daily price-return standard deviation, intraday cross-sectional dispersion, or annualized vol. A true 20–30% daily return vol would annualize to ~315–475% — extreme by any commodity standard and inconsistent with "healthy." The actual metric is ambiguous and should not be used to size hedges without clarification. - Published research (with Jefferson Lab, presented at a GPO conference) shows 38% performance variance for the same GPU chip across providers — the primary fungibility challenge and the strongest evidence for structural basis risk. Spot Price Signals - A100 rental prices up 10–15% in the past three months; B200 prices initially declined post-launch and have since recovered above launch price — both indicating demand/supply is tightening, not loosening. - Price per million tokens (blended input/output, consumption-weighted across 300 models tracked) has doubled since December 1, 2025 to approximately $2.21 — directly contradicting the consensus inference-deflation narrative. GPU Asset Economics - As of last year per Lee's data: second-year H100 residual value ~85 cents on the dollar; third-year ~84 cents. Lee explicitly contrasts this with car depreciation. Temporal caveat (QA correction): this is lagged data from the prior period; given rapid generational GPU turnover, the figure may not reflect current marks. Lee also has a commercial interest in high residual values (she operates a refurbished chip business). - Data center build announcements do not translate to immediate GPU availability; servers, colocation, and fiber are sequential dependencies. This is a specific, unstated pushback on the headline hyperscaler capex narrative. Institutional Participation - Some banks can cross positions internally; Lee wants dedicated compute trading desks but acknowledges GPU trading requires hardware, software, and regional supply/demand expertise — slowing desk formation. - Speculators are needed to provide liquidity, but financial settlement means early open interest will be dominated by directional bets, not hedgers — a standard early-stage commodity pattern. Best Quotes 1. On basis risk and index utility "This price will be highly correlated to the price you pay at a cloud provider. However, it won't be the same, just like basis trading in other commodities. There's a basis risk." — Carmen Lee Significance: The product's primary limitation, stated by its creator. Basis risk is structural, not solvable — PM must model this slippage before using CME futures as a procurement hedge. 2. On fungibility and the 38% variance "We proved there's a 38% performance variance for the same chip." — Carmen Lee Significance: The single most important structural risk to index integrity. An index averaging across a 38% performance spread produces a settlement price that may bear limited relation to any specific buyer's actual compute experience. 3. On token price inflation "The price for a million tokens has doubled since December 1st of last year to about $2.21, which is a mixture of input/output token prices average-weighted by consumption." — Carmen Lee Significance: Specific, dated, consumption-weighted data point directly contradicting the inference-commoditization consensus. Non-consensus in direction and magnitude. 4. On supply-chain friction in announced capacity "It's not that easy to bring any GPU online. You hear about big data center builds, but they don't translate to immediate GPU availability. You need the servers, colocation, and optical fiber. The stars have to be aligned."

title: 20VC — Perplexity CEO: Micron Will Be More Valuable Than Meta & How Export Controls Helped Not Hurt China
text: Perplexity / Aravind Srinivas — Research Memo Thesis The AI value stack is shifting from model capability to orchestration and interface ownership: whoever controls the layer that converts model intelligence into high-value output captures durable margin, while pure-play model providers face commoditization as open-source catches frontier. Power — not capital or chips — is the binding three-year constraint on AI capacity expansion, and the companies that own permitted, powered land extract structural scarcity rent. Perplexity's answer engine was always customer acquisition; the real business is agentic deep research, and revenue has more than tripled in 2026 YTD. Key Points Answer engine = lead gen, not the product. Pro/Max subscription revenue comes from deep research and agentic workflows, not search answers. Srinivas frames every early-stage AI product as a funnel into the frontier product layer. Google's AI Mode is a functional copy of Perplexity. Srinivas claims credit for changing Google's core interface — same font, inline citations, bolding, suggested follow-ups — and states it is "still not as good." He frames this as validation, not threat, because the frontier has already moved to agents. Google is specifically behind on coding models. Srinivas says Google "underestimated the importance of coding models, so they are behind the frontier right now" — a distinct, falsifiable, near-term call separate from the interface-copy argument. Chat interface is structurally incompatible with advertising. Top Google advertisers (Amazon, Booking.com, Expedia) depend on exploratory, vibes-based user intent — which flows to Meta/Instagram, not an objective answer engine. Explicitly bearish on a $100–200B ad business for OpenAI. Model commoditization is the central structural risk for AI labs. "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized." Open-source models closing on frontier quality within 12 months is presented as the expected case, not a tail risk. Orchestration is the differentiator; token value per watt per user is the key metric. Perplexity's claim: it orchestrates across models (not just tools/files), which Anthropic and OpenAI cannot do. This multi-model routing is the basis for its efficiency argument. Micron could exceed Meta's market cap in 6–12 months. Grounded in bottleneck logic: HBM is the binding constraint; whatever is the bottleneck commands the price. Phrased deliberately cautiously ("might not be inconceivable"). Power is the three-year bottleneck, and public resistance compounds it. Permitting, land, turbines, cooling — not capital — are the rate-limiters. Srinivas says resistance will "continue and get worse" based on misinformation about data center water/power consumption. Revenue more than tripled since January 2026. Only hard financial datapoint disclosed. No absolute figures given. Local/hybrid compute is the architecture for durable AI without "going bankrupt." Continuously learning local models reduce context-window costs and address privacy; Perplexity positions itself as the orchestrator across local + server. Team of 400 today; maybe 800–1,000 in two years. Argues AI enables multi-billion-dollar companies built with 40 people — capital efficiency thesis for the sector. OpenAI IPO financial readiness questioned — but only off-camera. Host attributes a pre-show comment to Srinivas that OpenAI isn't financially ready for an IPO. Srinivas deflects on-record without confirming or denying. Best Quotes 1. On Google's AI Mode as derivative: "Nobody ever wanted to ship an answer engine at Google. Nobody wanted to tinker with the interface that made them $250 billion a year. And now you look at AI mode, it looks exactly like Perplexity. There's not even any difference—the font, the citations, the specific bolding of inline text, inline hyperlinks, suggested follow-ups. The whole experience is literally looking like Perplexity, except it's still not as good." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Frames Google's AI Mode as defensive imitation, not innovation — and asserts quality inferiority. If accurate, implies sustained execution risk for Alphabet's search transition and an open window at the quality frontier. 2. On chat's structural incompatibility with advertising: "Who's the number one advertiser on Google? Amazon. Number two is Booking.com. Number three or four is Expedia. How do you book your hotels or flights? Do you book it on ChatGPT or Google? [Host: Google.] Exactly. The interface is less about conversations and more about exploration. When the decision-making is subjective and vibes-based, you don't need an objective answer engine. That's why I'm bearish on advertising taking off in the chat interface." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: A mechanistic argument — not a vibe — against the OpenAI advertising bull case. Travel/e-commerce, the two largest Google ad verticals, don't convert in a chat interface. 3. On orchestration as the true value layer: "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized. We differentiate ourselves at Perplexity because we don't just orchestrate across tools and files; we also orchestrate across models. That is the differentiation Anthropic and OpenAI cannot claim. We can increase the token value per watt per user. The most important metric in AI is token value per watt per user." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Names the sector's structural fault line and introduces a metric (token value per watt per user) that reframes how AI infrastructure and application companies should be evaluated. 4. On the Micron/Meta relative value call: "It might not be inconceivable that Micron, the supplier of HBM, might be more valuable than Meta in the next 6 to 12 months." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Deliberately hedged phrasing, but the bottleneck-rent logic is stated with higher conviction. Directionally actionable as a framework for relative posi

title: Yet Another Value — Adam May on $ABVX's blowout data and subsequent stock crash
text: Abivax (ABVX) & Nectar Therapeutics — Research Memo Recorded June 8, 2026 | Guest: Adam May, specialist biotech long/short investor Thesis Abivax's Phase 3 UC maintenance trial delivered best-in-class efficacy — matching Rinvoq on clinical remission delta and roughly doubling it on the GI-preferred endoscopic remission endpoint — without Rinvoq's black-box safety profile. The post-data collapse from ~$185 to ~$100 was driven by a cancer signal May argues is demonstrably noise: after reclassifying one non-cancer case and four non-melanoma skin cancers, only two common solid-tumor cancers remain with no mechanistic pathway. At ~$100, May believes the market is fully pricing in a black-box warning it may not receive, creating asymmetric skew he frames as 100% near-term upside and perhaps 200% over twelve months. Key Points Efficacy — the setup entering maintenance data - The prior induction trial ranked Abivax as the third most efficacious drug ever studied in ulcerative colitis — a high bar entering the maintenance readout. - May's own pre-release estimate was a 25% placebo-adjusted clinical remission delta; the actual result came in at 40% (50mg) and 39% (25mg) — a material upside surprise on his own conservative baseline. - The independent Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) had reviewed 80–90% of trial data before the readout with no new safety signals — making the post-release cancer surprise more anomalous, not less, and strengthening the statistical-noise argument. Efficacy vs. best-in-class comparator - Clinical remission delta matched/exceeded Rinvoq (JAK inhibitor), previously considered the ceiling for UC efficacy. - Endoscopic remission delta: Abivax 38% vs. Rinvoq 18% — approximately 2× on the endpoint GI physicians weight most because it is objective (scope-verified, not patient-reported). - Rinvoq carries a black-box warning for cancer, severe/fatal infections, blood clots, and cardiovascular events; Abivax does not currently carry one. The cancer signal — May's case-by-case decomposition - Raw headline: 7 cancer cases (high-dose arm) vs. 1 (placebo) — this is what drove the selloff. - Reclassification: 1 case was colonic dysplasia (precancerous condition, not cancer); 4 cases were non-melanoma skin cancer (15–20× more prevalent than other cancers, typically resolved in a 15-minute outpatient procedure). - Residual: 2 "real" cancers in the 50mg arm; 0 in the 25mg arm; 0 in placebo — common solid tumors (prostate, breast), no anatomical clustering. - Mechanistic argument: drug is neither genotoxic nor immunosuppressive; severe infections were actually more common in the placebo arm , which is the opposite of what immunosuppression would produce. - DSMB context (above) reinforces: an independent safety board saw nothing alarming through ~85% of the trial. - Management error: the inflated cancer count is partly self-inflicted — the presentation included non-cancer events in the cancer tally, triggering a selloff the underlying data does not support. Valuation / scenario framing - At ~$100 (as of June 8): May says this already fully prices in a black-box warning. - Blue-sky scenario (no black box + Crohn's disease approval): $8–10B peak sales potential. May describes the skew as "huge" but does not assign an explicit probability to the regulatory outcome. - Near-term downside limited by UC efficacy: the drug unambiguously works for ulcerative colitis — that is not in dispute and sets a floor. - Key residual bear risk May acknowledges: Part 2 data could add cancer cases; market is partly waiting on that. Why the mispricing persists - Analytical barrier: reconstructing the case-level cancer count requires work most market participants haven't done. - Sell-side downgrade cascade: mechanical, coverage-driven — not necessarily based on case-level reclassification. - Part 2 fear: investors may be holding off pending the next data drop. Nectar Therapeutics (no ticker confirmed in transcript) - Stock pulled back from ~$100 to mid-$50s with no fundamental change to the alopecia areata signal. - May attributes weakness to: (1) ongoing jury trial litigation vs. Eli Lilly — outside typical biotech investor frameworks, creating holder mismatch; (2) competitive overhang from Q32 Bio hyping their own alopecia areata program. - May says "I'm at a loss as to why the sell-off has been so severe" — admits incomplete explanatory model. - Ranked explicitly as the less mispriced of the two positions; Abivax is the priority call. Best Quotes 1. The efficacy headline "Abivax's maintenance data came in with a 'four handle'—40% at the high dose and 39% at the low dose. It matched and exceeded Rinvoq on clinical remission delta. Even more impressively, on endoscopic remission, which is a more objective endpoint that GI doctors favor, Abivax crushed Rinvoq, with a 38% delta compared to Rinvoq's 18%." — Adam May Significance: The 2× endoscopic remission advantage is the buried lead. This is the endpoint prescribers trust most, and it is directly relevant to real-world adoption independent of label language. 2. Dismantling the cancer signal "You are left with two 'real' cancers in the 50mg arm, zero in the 25mg arm, and zero in placebo. These two were common cancers—prostate and breast—with no clustering. There is no 'smoking gun' mechanism for how this drug would cause cancer; it is not genotoxic, and it is not immunosuppressive, as severe infections were more common in the placebo arm. This is statistical noise." — Adam May Significance: The mechanistic argument is more durable than a statistical one — it is testable at FDA and in the literature, and it directly attacks the bear thesis at its foundation. 3. Why the market is wrong without being irrational "I don't believe in efficient markets. I'm amazed at the things the market is able to ignore. It takes a lot of work to calculate these numbers, and I think people either haven't done it or are worried that more cases will come out in the part two data." —

title: Yet Another Value — Alex Roepers on two deep-value special situations: $DCH and $NOMD
text: DCH & Nomad Foods — Research Memo Guest: Alex Roers, Atlantic Investment | Host: Andrew Walker, Yet Another Value Podcast Thesis DCH (American Axle + DLE merger, ~$6.32) is a catalyst-driven deep value situation where the market is pricing ICE-supplier pessimism without credit for a credible $300M EBITDA synergy target that represents only ~3% of combined revenue; rough EPS power of ~$1.50 implies a 4x earnings multiple with a board-endorsed PSU structure anchoring management to $12–$22. Nomad Foods (~$10.21, down from $30) is a "paid to wait" frozen food compounder trading below 7x EBITDA with a 7% dividend yield, insider buying at current levels, and a governance structure that does not preclude a PE takeout — but it is explicitly a "show me" story requiring operational execution from a new CEO. Key Points DCH - Formed via merger of American Axle (US) and DLE (formerly GKN Automotive, spun from Melrose Industries in ~2018–2019); ~$11B combined revenue, listed NYSE at ~$6.32 - Atlantic was an activist in GKN in 2018, pushed the aerospace/automotive split, benefited from Melrose's hostile bid, then re-engaged the automotive stub (DLE) in 2023 with the same playbook - Atlantic also holds Aptiv (APTV) and Continental (CON.DE) — guest disclosed this while discussing naming conventions; relevant context for their broader auto-supplier thesis and as a conflict-of-interest disclosure - Synergy target: $300M+ EBITDA; guest breaks down as ~30% SG&A (duplicate officers, public company costs, workforce), remainder from purchasing scale and 170-plant footprint rationalization; 3% of $11B sales framing is the credibility anchor - EPS power: guest cited "being very rough with numbers, $1.50" — this is a directional placeholder, not a modeled estimate - FCF: zero modeled in 2026 due to integration costs; 2027–2028 are the true cash generation years - Leverage: ~3x debt/EBITDA; Atlantic's sequenced playbook is delever to <2.5x first, then push for buybacks - PSU structure (host's pre-call discovery via Feb 3, 2026 8-K, confirmed by Roers): CEO package begins vesting at $12, scales to $22, over a ~3.5-year window — host frames this as the board's own price target range; Roers agreed there is "good alignment of interest" - Return framing: "double or triple in the next year and a half to two years" if synergies execute — guest's words, contingent on execution and macro Nomad Foods (NOMD) - $3.5B revenue, all European frozen food (Birds Eye and equivalent brands); trades ~$10.21 vs. $30 in 2021 - Metrics: <7x EBITDA, ~7% dividend yield, ~$1.50 EPS (forecasted — transcript does not specify the source) - $90M/year dividend; guest says it does not need to be cut — cash flow covers it; natural compression if stock re-rates to $15–$20 - Insider buying: Noam Gottesman recently purchased a "large number of shares" at ~$10 (named specifically) - New CEO installed (prior CEO departed end of 2024); known headwinds: private label inroads from Aldi, volume pressure, need for marketing/R&D reinvestment - Guest explicitly labels it a "show me" story ; comfort rests on new CEO, insider buying, and dividend floor — not demonstrated operational recovery - M&A optionality: guest frames Nomad as a PE takeout candidate; key governance point — Martin Franklin and associates are key shareholders but do not control the company , removing a structural veto on a sale - European discount: guest de-emphasizes the valuation drag rather than dismissing it; adds geopolitical resolution as an unquantified upside optionality for European multiples broadly Best Quotes 1. DCH return thesis in one sentence "In our view, this company can earn, being very rough with numbers, $1.50. It's a $6 stock; if they do a good job with synergies and things go their way economically, you're looking at a double or triple on the stock in the next year and a half to two years." — Alex Roers Anchors the entire DCH thesis: EPS placeholder ($1.50, explicitly rough), current price, and time horizon in a single statement. The "very rough" qualifier is load-bearing — treat this as a directional anchor, not a model output. 2. Synergy credibility framing "This is only 3% of $11 billion in sales. It is very achievable." — Alex Roers Directly addresses the most common bear pushback on merger synergy targets; context-sizes the ask against the revenue base. 3. 2026 is noise — hear it from the horse "We have zero free cash flow modeled for this year due to integration costs. 2027 and 2028 will be the years they really crank out cash." — Alex Roers Explicit signal to ignore 2026 FCF as a thesis data point; sets the clock for when results will matter. 4. Franklin governance point — the overlooked unlock "They don't control the company. They are key shareholders, but I imagine they don't like the price at $10." — Alex Roers Removes the primary structural impediment to a Nomad takeout. Franklin's inability to block a sale is a non-obvious governance point most holders may underweight when assessing M&A optionality. Roers' actual rebuttal: "coming from 1%, he's not going to own a lot more, and if he achieves the stock appreciation we expect, he's aligning the interests pretty well" — i.e., the appreciation itself creates alignment. title: a16z Podcast — The Economics of AI Usage and What's Next For SaaS | Benedict Evans on a16z
text: AI Eats the World (Benedict Evans, Updated Presentation) — Research Memo Thesis Foundation models have no sustainable moat — no network effects, no data lock-in, no leverage analogous to Google Search — making commoditization the null hypothesis that bulls must disprove. Value will accrue above the model layer, in tooling, configuration, and vertical workflow software, not at the model itself. Agentic coding is the only confirmed product-market-fit use case; every other application remains unproven at consumer scale, with Evans explicitly stating he sees no path to daily consumer usage "with the technology we have right now." Key Points Confirmed PMF — Coding Only - Agentic coding crossed from "kind of useful" to "pulling it out of your hands" at the beginning of this year (year inferred from context; Evans says "the beginning of this year"). All other use cases remain unproven at consumer scale. - Evans's explanation for why coding was first: software developers were the early adopters; they naturally automated their own work. Analogous to PCs in the early 80s — the first thing people did with the technology was build more of it. Consumer Adoption — A Material Caveat - Evans explicitly states: "We don't see a way that consumers will use this daily rather than weekly with the technology we have right now." This is a direct constraint on any bull case for consumer-facing AI applications. Model Commodity Thesis — Burden of Proof, Not Conviction - Evans frames this as a Socratic challenge: "It's not that I know they're going to become commodities; my position is that the argument for them becoming commodities is strong, so explain to me why they won't be." - Structural basis: no network effects, no differentiated data moat, no leverage, competitive difference reducible to willingness to spend capital. - Trillion-to-two-trillion dollars of capex in the pipeline; models improving 100x–200x in efficiency per year; no source of price discipline identified. - Historical analog: mobile data in 2009–2010 — pricing crises resolved by alignment with underlying cost. - Complication Evans raises but does not resolve: could also end up like semiconductors — fewer players as each generation gets more expensive to build, which is oligopoly, not commodity. Chatbot Is V1 UI, Not a Product - Requires tooling, right data, and configuration. Enterprise buyers don't "standardize on Claude" — model selection is abstracted away. Foundation models look like hyperscalers: infrastructure without leverage. SaaS Apocalypse - Cheaper, faster software creation multiplies competition across every vertical. Evans is explicit that some incumbents will be wiped out; he cannot identify which ones. He hedges: the LLM may be both a feature inside Salesforce and a synthesis layer above all data — "the answer is probably both." Enterprise AI ROI — Measurement Problem, Not Pullback - ROI is structurally hard to measure at this stage. Benefits manifest as competitive necessity (same output, fewer people) rather than new revenue lines. Evans cautions against reading this as a pullback signal: companies that stop spending risk falling behind competitors who don't. Tacit Organizational Knowledge as Deployment Bottleneck - Much of what organizations do is undocumented. Consulting firms have value precisely because they surface how things actually work versus how they're supposed to work. This is difficult to bake into AI tools — a material constraint on enterprise AI deployment speed. Non-Coding Enterprise PMF Is Emerging Narrowly - Evans spoke days before the recording with a commodities company using LLMs to improve cash-flow predictions — a specific, margin-constrained vertical use case. This is evidence that non-coding PMF is appearing in narrow, structured-prediction applications, not uniformly absent. Next Consequential Questions Are Industry-Specific, Not Technical - Law firm pyramid economics; Hollywood labor under generative video; advertising intent understanding. These are media-industry and professional-services questions, not San Francisco tech questions. - Unlike prior platform shifts, the performance ceiling of generative AI is genuinely unknown — in 1995 you knew telcos couldn't deliver broadband next week; no equivalent physical constraint exists here. On-Device / Open-Source as Forward Risk - Evans raises (as a forward question, not a present reality): at what point are open-source or on-device models good enough that workloads migrate off expensive cloud inference? No timeline given. Best Quotes 1. "There's no clear, sustainable, differentiated way to build a model that's fundamentally better than everyone else's. There's no network effect. There are no levers to pull like Google Search or YouTube. There isn't a fundamental competitive difference except your willingness to spend money." — Benedict Evans Significance: The core bear case on foundation model economics in one sentence. Moat = capital, which structurally limits pricing power and long-run margins for pure-play labs. 2. "We've got a trillion or two trillion dollars of capex coming down the pipe, models are getting 100x to 200x more efficient every year, and they're all kind of doing the same thing. Why would they have pricing power?" — Benedict Evans Significance: Combines massive supply-side build with exponential efficiency gains — the two forces most likely to compress AI infrastructure pricing — as a single rhetorical challenge to infrastructure bulls. 3. "Anthropic, with less capital raised, said, 'No, we're going to focus on coding,' and they got it working. Whether that was a deliberate strategy or they stumbled into it is for others to say, but it worked." — Benedict Evans Significance: Frames Anthropic's coding focus as potentially emergent rather than deliberate — a direct challenge to narratives of strategic foresight, and relevant to assessing durability of their competitive position. 4.
